slides.narration: Almost all the mass of an atom sits in a nucleus a hundred thousand times smaller across than the atom itself. In this chapter we ask what the nucleus is made of, how large and how dense it is, and why it weighs less than the sum of its parts. The answer to the last question, through Einstein’s relation between mass and energy, is the key to nuclear power.

slides.heading: What is inside a nucleus
slides.body_md: A nucleus contains **protons** (charge +e) and **neutrons** (no charge), together called **nucleons**. A nuclide is written $^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$, with $A = Z + N$.
bullets: Z is the atomic number (protons), N the neutron number, A the mass number (nucleons).
The number of electrons in the neutral atom is Z, so Z decides the chemical element.
Protons repel one another electrically; the short-range **strong nuclear force** holds the nucleons together.

rows: Number of neutrons, N = A − Z
Number of nucleons, A = Z + N
A written above Z, before the element symbol

visual.alt: Table of atomic number, neutron number and mass number, each with its symbol, meaning and its value for sodium-23

slides.narration: A nucleus is built of protons and neutrons, which we call nucleons. The number of protons is the atomic number. The number of nucleons is the mass number, and the neutron number is the difference. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, so the atomic number decides the element. Protons repel each other, so something stronger must hold the nucleus together: the strong nuclear force.

slides.heading: Isotopes, isobars and isotones
slides.body_md: Nuclides are grouped by what they share:
bullets: **Isotopes:** same Z, different A (same element, same chemistry), such as carbon-12 and carbon-13.
**Isobars:** same A, different Z, such as carbon-13 and nitrogen-13.
**Isotones:** same N, different Z, such as carbon-12 and nitrogen-13.

visual.alt: Table of isotopes, isobars and isotones: what is the same and what differs, with an example pair for each

slides.narration: Nuclides that share one number are given a family name. Isotopes have the same number of protons, so they are the same element, but different numbers of neutrons. Isobars have the same mass number but different elements. Isotones have the same number of neutrons. In the picture, carbon twelve and carbon thirteen are isotopes, carbon thirteen and nitrogen thirteen are isobars, and carbon twelve and nitrogen thirteen are isotones.

slides.heading: Size of the nucleus
slides.body_md:
Experiments with fast particles show that the radius of a nucleus of mass number A is
$$R = R_0A^{1/3},\qquad R_0 \approx 1.2\ \text{fm} = 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}.$$
bullets: Radii run from about 1.9 fm (helium-4) to about 7.4 fm (uranium-238): a nucleus is about 10⁵ times smaller across than its atom.
R ∝ A^(1/3) means volume ∝ A: each nucleon takes up the same volume, as in a tightly packed drop of liquid.

visual.alt: Graph of nuclear radius in femtometres against the cube root of the mass number: a straight line through the origin with slope 1.2 femtometres; marked points are A equals 4 with R 1.9 fm, A equals 16 with 3.0 fm, A equals 64 with 4.8 fm and A equals 208 with 7.1 fm
visual.caption: R is proportional to A^(1/3): the volume of a nucleus is proportional to its number of nucleons.

slides.narration: The radius of a nucleus is found to grow as the cube root of the mass number, with a constant of about one point two femtometres. A femtometre is ten to the minus fifteen metres. So a nucleus of a hundred and twenty five nucleons is only five times wider than a single proton. Because the radius goes as the cube root, the volume is proportional to the number of nucleons.

slides.narration: The cube root of sixty four is exactly four, so the radius is four point eight femtometres. The volume of that sphere is about four point six times ten to the minus forty three cubic metres. The mass is sixty four nucleons, about one point one times ten to the minus twenty five kilograms. Dividing gives a density of about two point three times ten to the seventeen kilograms per cubic metre.

slides.heading: Nuclear density is the same for all nuclei
slides.body_md:
Mass of a nucleus $\approx Am$ (m = mass of a nucleon); volume $= \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3A$. Hence
$$\rho = \dfrac{Am}{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3A} = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}$$
bullets: A cancels: the density is the same for every nucleus, about 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
This is about 10¹⁴ times the density of water: a matchbox of nuclear matter would weigh billions of tonnes.
It shows that nucleons are packed at a fixed spacing, whatever the size of the nucleus.

slides.narration: To compare densities, divide mass by volume. The mass of a nucleus is the mass number times the mass of one nucleon. Its volume is also proportional to the mass number. So the mass number cancels, and the density equals three times the nucleon mass divided by four pi times R naught cubed. It is the same for every nucleus: about two point three times ten to the seventeen kilograms per cubic metre.

slides.heading: The unified atomic mass unit
slides.body_md: The **unified atomic mass unit** (u) is one twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom: $1\ \text{u} = 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}$ kg.
bullets: By definition the atomic mass of carbon-12 is exactly 12 u.
Masses of nuclides are quoted as atomic masses (nucleus plus electrons) in u.
A proton and a neutron each have a mass of about 1 u.

visual.alt: Table of the masses of the proton, neutron, hydrogen atom and electron in unified atomic mass units and their rest energies in megaelectronvolts

slides.narration: Kilograms are far too large for nuclei, so we use the unified atomic mass unit. It is defined as one twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon twelve atom, which makes the mass of carbon twelve exactly twelve of these units. One unit is about one point six six times ten to the minus twenty seven kilograms. Protons and neutrons weigh about one unit each, and an electron only about one two-thousandth of that.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the energy equivalent of one atomic mass unit
slides.body_md: Einstein: a mass m is equivalent to energy $E = mc^2$. Find the energy of 1 u in joules and in MeV. ($c = 2.998 \times 10^{8}$ m s⁻¹, 1 eV $= 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ J)
bullets: We use 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c² throughout (the accepted value; rounded constants give 931.6).

visual.alt: Table of the masses of the proton, neutron, hydrogen atom and electron in unified atomic mass units and their rest energies in megaelectronvolts

slides.narration: Einstein’s relation says that any mass m is equivalent to an energy m times c squared. Put in one atomic mass unit and the speed of light, and you get about one point four nine times ten to the minus ten joules. Divide by the joules in one megaelectronvolt and the answer is about nine hundred and thirty one point five megaelectronvolts. That is the conversion factor we use for the rest of the chapter.

slides.heading: Mass defect and binding energy
slides.body_md:
The mass of a stable nucleus is **less** than the total mass of its separate nucleons. The difference is the **mass defect**:
$$\Delta m = Zm_p + (A - Z)m_n - m_{\text{nucleus}}$$
The energy equivalent is the **binding energy**, $B = \Delta m\,c^2$ = the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart into free nucleons (and the energy released when it forms).
bullets: With atomic masses use $Z\,m_H$ instead of $Zm_p$: the electron masses cancel.
B (in MeV) = Δm (in u) × 931.5.
Binding energy per nucleon = B/A.

slides.heading: Pair production
slides.body_md:
A gamma-ray photon can turn into an electron and a positron (same mass, charge +e), converting energy into mass:
$$h\nu \ge 2m_ec^2 = 2 \times 0.511 = 1.022\ \text{MeV}$$
bullets: It happens only near a nucleus, which takes up momentum so that energy and momentum are both conserved; a photon alone in empty space cannot do it.
Any energy above 1.022 MeV appears as kinetic energy of the pair.
Photon wavelength at the threshold: about 1.21 pm.

slides.narration: Energy can become mass. A gamma ray passing close to a nucleus can turn into an electron and a positron, a particle of the same mass but positive charge. Each needs its rest energy, zero point five one one megaelectronvolts, so the photon must carry at least one point zero two two. The nucleus is needed to take up momentum. Any extra energy becomes motion of the pair.

slides.heading: Annihilation
slides.body_md: When an electron and a positron meet, they **annihilate**: their whole mass becomes radiation.
bullets: At rest, two photons of 0.511 MeV each leave in **opposite directions**: one photon could not conserve momentum.
The photon wavelength is $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E} = \dfrac{1240\ \text{MeV fm}}{0.511\ \text{MeV}} = 2.43$ pm.
It is the reverse of pair production, and a clean example of mass turning into energy: the basis of PET scanners.

slides.narration: Annihilation is the reverse. An electron and a positron meet and disappear, leaving two gamma rays. If they were at rest, momentum was zero before, so the photons must go off in opposite directions, and each carries zero point five one one megaelectronvolts. This is the clearest example of all the mass of matter turning into energy, and it is used in medical PET scanners.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Z protons, N neutrons, A = Z + N nucleons
$R = R_0A^{1/3}$, R₀ = 1.2 fm; density $\dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}$ kg m⁻³ for all nuclei
Δm = Zm_H + (A − Z)mₙ − M; B = Δm × 931.5 MeV
Pair production needs ≥ 1.022 MeV; annihilation gives two 0.511 MeV photons

visual.alt: Summary table of nuclear composition, size and density, the mass-energy relation, mass defect and binding energy, and pair production and annihilation

slides.narration: To sum up: a nucleus has protons and neutrons, its radius grows as the cube root of the mass number, and its density is the same for every nucleus. One atomic mass unit is equivalent to nine hundred and thirty one point five megaelectronvolts. The mass defect of a nucleus gives its binding energy. And a photon of at least one point zero two two megaelectronvolts can make an electron and a positron.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Use atomic masses with $m_H$, not $m_p$, and say so; the electron masses cancel.
Keep six decimal places in u until the final multiplication by 931.5: the mass defect is a small difference of large numbers.
For the density proof, show that A cancels; do not just quote the value.
Pair production: say that the nucleus is needed for momentum; annihilation: two photons, opposite directions.

rows: Same Z / same A / same N

slides.narration: When working out a binding energy, use atomic masses with the hydrogen atom mass, not the proton mass, so that the electrons cancel. Keep six decimal places until the last step. To show that nuclear density is constant, show the mass number cancelling. And for pair production remember the nucleus, which takes up momentum, while annihilation at rest always gives two photons in opposite directions.

slides.narration: Why can energy be got both by splitting the heaviest nuclei and by joining the lightest ones? The answer is in a single graph, the binding energy per nucleon plotted against mass number. In this part we read that graph, then meet fission in reactors and bombs and fusion in the Sun and the hydrogen bomb.

slides.heading: The binding energy per nucleon curve
slides.body_md: Binding energy per nucleon, B/A, measures how tightly each nucleon is held. Plotted against A for real nuclides:
bullets: It rises steeply for light nuclei (about 1.1 MeV for ²H), with a peak at ⁴He (7.07 MeV).
It reaches a **maximum of about 8.8 MeV** near A = 56–62 (iron, nickel).
It then falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV for uranium.
Between A about 30 and 170 it is nearly flat, within about 10% of 8.5 MeV.

slides.narration: Here is the curve, computed from real atomic masses. Binding energy per nucleon climbs very steeply for the lightest nuclei, has a bump at helium four, and peaks at about eight point eight megaelectronvolts for nuclei near iron and nickel. Beyond that it falls slowly, to about seven point six for uranium. In the middle, between about thirty and a hundred and seventy, it is almost constant.

slides.heading: Stability of middle-order nuclei
slides.body_md: The higher B/A, the more tightly bound the nucleus, the more stable. So the **middle-order nuclei** (A about 50 to 80) are the most stable.
bullets: Nearly constant B/A: each nucleon bonds only with its near neighbours (the strong force is short-range and saturates).
The fall beyond A about 60: the electrostatic repulsion between protons acts across the whole nucleus and grows faster than the number of nucleons.
A nucleus moving **towards** the maximum releases energy.

visual.alt: Table of the three regions of the binding energy per nucleon curve with typical values, the process that raises the binding energy per nucleon and whether energy is released

slides.narration: Why is the curve flat in the middle? The strong force has a short range, so each nucleon bonds only with its nearest neighbours, and adding more nucleons adds the same binding each. Why does it fall at the end? The electric repulsion between protons acts across the whole nucleus, so it grows faster than the number of nucleons. Moving towards the peak always releases energy.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a heavy nucleus splits in two
slides.body_md: A nucleus of mass number 236 with B/A = 7.6 MeV splits into two equal fragments of mass number 118, each with B/A = 8.5 MeV. Estimate the energy released.
bullets: Total binding energy before: $236 \times 7.6 = 1794$ MeV.
After: $2 \times 118 \times 8.5 = 2006$ MeV.
Energy released $= 2006 - 1794 = 212.4$ MeV $\approx 212$ MeV, about 200 MeV.

slides.heading: Nuclear fission
slides.body_md:
In **fission** a heavy nucleus, after absorbing a slow neutron, splits into two middle-order fragments and releases neutrons and about 200 MeV:
$$ ^{1}_{0}\text{n} + {}^{235}_{92}\text{U} \to {}^{141}_{56}\text{Ba} + {}^{92}_{36}\text{Kr} + 3\,^{1}_{0}\text{n} + Q$$
bullets: Balance: the nucleon numbers (1 + 235 = 141 + 92 + 3) and the charges (92 = 56 + 36) match on both sides.
Fragments differ from event to event; on average 2 to 3 neutrons are released.
Almost all the energy appears as kinetic energy of the fragments, then as heat.

slides.heading: The chain reaction
slides.body_md: The neutrons released can cause further fissions: a **chain reaction**.
bullets: **Uncontrolled:** each fission leads on average to more than one further fission, so the rate grows enormously in a tiny fraction of a second (a bomb).
**Controlled:** only about one neutron per fission goes on to cause another; the rest escape or are absorbed, so the rate stays steady (a reactor).
Details of the chain reaction are not required by the ISC syllabus.

slides.narration: The neutrons set free by one fission can strike other uranium nuclei and cause more fissions: a chain reaction. If each fission causes more than one further fission, the number grows very quickly, doubling again and again: this is uncontrolled, and it is a bomb. If on average just one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another, the rate stays steady: this is controlled, and it is a reactor.

slides.narration: This is a schematic reactor. The fuel rods, made of enriched uranium, stand in a moderator. Control rods can slide in and out between them. A coolant is pumped through the core, leaves hot, and passes its heat to a heat exchanger that makes steam for a turbine. Thick concrete and steel shielding surrounds everything, to stop neutrons and gamma rays.

slides.heading: Parts of a reactor and their functions
slides.body_md: Each part has one job:
bullets: Fast neutrons are poor at causing fission in U-235: the moderator slows them by collisions with light nuclei.
Pushing the control rods in absorbs more neutrons and lowers the power; pulling them out raises it.

rows: Nuclei that fission and release energy
Slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds so they cause fission
Absorb neutrons; moved in or out to hold the rate steady or shut down
Carries the heat out of the core to make steam
Water, heavy water, liquid sodium, carbon dioxide
Absorbs neutrons and gamma rays to protect people

visual.alt: Table of the parts of a nuclear reactor, the function of each and a typical material

slides.narration: Each part has one job. The fuel provides nuclei that fission. The moderator slows fast neutrons, because slow neutrons are much better at causing fission in uranium two three five. Control rods of cadmium or boron absorb neutrons, and moving them in or out keeps the rate steady or shuts the reactor down. The coolant takes heat away, and the shielding protects people.

slides.heading: The nuclear bomb
slides.body_md: A fission bomb is an **uncontrolled** chain reaction in a compact mass of highly enriched uranium or plutonium: the energy of a very large number of fissions is released in a tiny fraction of a second.
bullets: A reactor has no such explosive chain reaction: its fuel is only slightly enriched and the control rods hold the neutron count steady.
The explosion releases heat, blast and dangerous radiation.

slides.narration: A fission bomb is a chain reaction with no control at all. A compact mass of highly enriched uranium or plutonium is brought together, the neutrons multiply from one generation to the next, and all the energy is released in a tiny fraction of a second. A reactor is quite different: its fuel is only slightly enriched, and control rods hold the number of neutrons steady, so it cannot explode like a bomb.

slides.heading: Nuclear fusion
slides.body_md: In **fusion**, two light nuclei join to form a heavier one, and energy is released because the product has a higher binding energy per nucleon. Inside the Sun, the net result of the **proton–proton chain** is four hydrogen nuclei becoming one helium nucleus:
bullets: About 26.7 MeV is released per helium nucleus formed, counting the positrons annihilating with electrons (the neutrinos carry off a little).
This **thermonuclear energy** powers the Sun and stars for billions of years.

rows: 0.42 MeV (1.44 MeV with the positron annihilating)

visual.alt: Table of the proton-proton chain that powers the Sun: three steps and the net result of four hydrogen nuclei becoming one helium nucleus with 26.7 megaelectronvolts released

slides.narration: In fusion, light nuclei join. In the Sun, four hydrogen nuclei are turned, in three steps, into one helium nucleus, with two positrons and two neutrinos. The helium is lighter than four protons, and the difference, equal to about twenty six point seven megaelectronvolts, is released each time. Energy from fusion at high temperature is called thermonuclear energy, and it keeps the Sun and stars shining for billions of years.

slides.heading: Why fusion needs very high temperatures
slides.body_md: Two nuclei are both positive, so they repel. To fuse they must get within about 10⁻¹⁵ m, where the strong force takes over: they must climb the **Coulomb barrier**.
bullets: Two protons just touching (centres 2.4 fm apart) have U = 1.44/2.4 = 0.60 MeV.
Only a gas at millions of kelvin has nuclei moving fast enough; hence **thermonuclear** reactions.

slides.narration: Why do nuclei need such high temperatures? Both are positively charged, so they repel, and they only fuse when they get as close as the range of the strong force. Climbing that barrier needs about six tenths of a megaelectronvolt for two protons. The mean thermal energy at fifteen million kelvin is a few hundred times smaller, so only the fastest nuclei get through. Hence the need for such enormous temperatures.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: how hot is hot enough?
slides.body_md: Two protons just touch when their centres are 2.4 fm apart. Find the electrostatic potential energy, and the temperature at which the mean kinetic energy (3/2)kT equals it. Compare with the mean energy at 1.5 × 10⁷ K. (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹)
bullets: $\dfrac{3}{2}kT = U \Rightarrow T = \dfrac{2 \times 9.60 \times 10^{-14}}{3 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23}} = 4.64 \times 10^{9}$ K.
At $1.5 \times 10^{7}$ K: $\dfrac{3}{2}kT = 1941$ eV, about 309 times smaller than the barrier: only the fastest nuclei in the hot gas can fuse.

slides.narration: Add the masses. Deuterium plus helium three weighs five point zero three zero one three one atomic mass units. slides.heading: Stars and the hydrogen bomb
slides.body_md: In the Sun and stars, gravity compresses hydrogen until its core is hot enough for fusion; the energy released keeps the core hot and the star shining.
bullets: A **hydrogen bomb** uses a fission bomb to supply the temperature of millions of kelvin needed to fuse isotopes of hydrogen: uncontrolled fusion.
Fusion gives more energy per nucleon than fission, but a steady, controlled fusion reactor on Earth has not yet been achieved.

rows: A heavy nucleus splits into two middle-order nuclei
Two light nuclei join into a heavier nucleus
A slow neutron to start it
A few MeV to about 25 MeV
The Sun, stars and hydrogen bombs

slides.narration: Stars hold their gas together by gravity, which compresses and heats the core until hydrogen fuses; the energy released keeps the core hot. A hydrogen bomb copies this: a fission bomb goes off first, and its heat and pressure make hydrogen isotopes fuse in an uncontrolled way. Fusion releases more energy per nucleon than fission, but nobody has yet built a steady fusion power station.

sections.heading: 1. Composition of the nucleus; isotopes, isobars and isotones
sections.body_md:
- A nucleus contains **protons** (charge +e) and **neutrons** (uncharged), together called **nucleons**. Atomic number Z = number of protons; neutron number N; mass number A = Z + N. A nuclide is written $^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$.
- **Isotopes:** same Z, different A and N (same element). **Isobars:** same A, different Z. **Isotones:** same N, different Z.
- The protons repel one another electrically; the **strong nuclear force** (short-range, attractive, the same between any two nucleons) holds the nucleus together.
- The **unified atomic mass unit** u is 1/12 of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom: 1 u = 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

sections.heading: 2. Size and density of the nucleus
sections.body_md:
- Nuclear radius: $R = R_0A^{1/3}$ with $R_0 \approx 1.2$ fm (1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m). Radii: about 1.9 fm for ⁴He, 4.8 fm for ⁶⁴Zn, about 7.4 fm for ²³⁸U; a nucleus is about 10⁵ times smaller across than its atom.
- Volume $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \propto A$: every nucleon occupies the same volume.
- **Density** $\rho = \dfrac{Am}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3A} = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}$: independent of A. About 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³ (with R₀ = 1.2 fm and m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg), some 10¹⁴ times the density of water.

key_terms.definition_md: The mass per unit volume of nuclear matter; about 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, the same for every nucleus.

sections.heading: 3. Mass–energy relation, mass defect and binding energy
sections.body_md:
- **Mass–energy relation:** a mass m is equivalent to energy $E = mc^2$. **1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²** (this value is used throughout; 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J).
- **Mass defect:** $\Delta m = Zm_p + (A - Z)m_n - m_{\text{nucleus}}$. With atomic masses: $\Delta m = Zm_H + (A - Z)m_n - M_{\text{atom}}$ (the electron masses cancel).
- **Binding energy:** $B = \Delta m\,c^2$ = the energy needed to separate the nucleus into free nucleons = the energy released when it forms. $B$ (MeV) $= \Delta m$ (u) $\times\ 931.5$. **Binding energy per nucleon** $= B/A$.
- Example: ²⁰Ne (19.992440 u): Δm = 0.17246 u, B = 160.6 MeV, B/A = 8.03 MeV.

key_terms.definition_md: The amount by which the mass of a nucleus is less than the total mass of its separate nucleons.
The energy equivalent of the mass defect: the energy needed to separate a nucleus into its nucleons.

sections.heading: 4. Pair production and annihilation
sections.body_md:
- **Pair production:** a gamma photon of energy $h\nu \ge 2m_ec^2 = 1.022$ MeV becomes an electron and a positron, in the field of a nucleus (which takes up momentum). Energy above 1.022 MeV is the kinetic energy of the pair.
- **Annihilation:** an electron and a positron meeting (at rest) change completely into two photons of 0.511 MeV each, moving in opposite directions (so that momentum is conserved); wavelength $\lambda = hc/E = 2.43$ pm.
- Both processes are direct evidence that mass and energy are equivalent.

The change of an electron and a positron into radiation (two photons of 0.511 MeV when at rest).

sections.heading: 5. Binding energy per nucleon curve; stability; why fission and fusion release energy
sections.body_md:
- B/A rises steeply for light nuclei (1.1 MeV for ²H; 7.07 MeV for ⁴He), has a maximum of about **8.8 MeV near A = 56–62** (iron, nickel), then falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV for uranium. Between A about 30 and 170 it is nearly constant.
- The **middle-order nuclei** are the most tightly bound and the most stable. The short-range strong force explains the flat part; the long-range repulsion of the protons explains the fall at large A.
- **Both fission and fusion move nuclei towards the maximum**: heavy nuclei split into middle-order fragments, light nuclei join into heavier ones. Higher B/A means the total binding energy increases, and the difference is released.
- **Estimate for fission:** energy released = A × (B/A of the fragments − B/A of the heavy nucleus). For A = 236 splitting into two halves with 7.6 and 8.5 MeV per nucleon: 236 × 0.9 ≈ 212 MeV.

sections.heading: 6. Nuclear fission, chain reaction, reactor and bomb
sections.body_md:
- **Fission:** a heavy nucleus (such as ²³⁵U) absorbs a slow neutron and splits into two middle-order fragments, with 2–3 neutrons and about 200 MeV. Example: ¹₀n + ²³⁵₉₂U → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3 ¹₀n, Q = 173.3 MeV (A and Z balance).
- **Chain reaction:** the neutrons cause further fissions. Uncontrolled (more than one further fission each): explosive, a **nuclear bomb**. Controlled (one on average): steady, a **reactor**.
- **Reactor:** **fuel** (enriched uranium); **moderator** (heavy water, graphite) slows neutrons so they cause fission; **control rods** (cadmium, boron) absorb neutrons, moved in or out to regulate the rate; **coolant** carries the heat to a heat exchanger and turbine; **shielding** (concrete, steel) absorbs neutrons and gamma rays.
- A reactor cannot explode like a bomb: its fuel is only slightly enriched and the control rods keep the chain reaction controlled.
- Not examined (removed in ISC): details of the chain reaction and quantitative reactor operation.

key_terms.definition_md: The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two middle-order nuclei, with the release of neutrons and a large amount of energy.
A material of light nuclei (such as heavy water or graphite) that slows fast neutrons so they can cause fission.
Rods of a neutron absorber (cadmium, boron) moved in or out of the core to regulate the chain reaction.

sections.heading: 7. Nuclear fusion; the Sun and stars; the hydrogen bomb
sections.body_md:
- **Fusion:** two light nuclei join into a heavier one, raising B/A and releasing energy. Example: ²₁H + ³₂He → ⁴₂He + ¹₁H, Q = 18.35 MeV.
- **High temperature:** both nuclei are positive and repel; to get within about 10⁻¹⁵ m they must climb the Coulomb barrier (0.60 MeV for two touching protons), so the gas must be at millions of kelvin: **thermonuclear** reactions. At 1.5 × 10⁷ K the mean energy is only about 2 keV; fusion proceeds because the fastest nuclei in the hot gas have far more than the mean.
- **Sun and stars:** the proton–proton chain turns four hydrogen nuclei into one helium nucleus, releasing about 26.7 MeV and keeping the star shining for billions of years.
- **Hydrogen bomb:** a fission bomb supplies the temperature to start uncontrolled fusion of hydrogen isotopes.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Use atomic masses with $m_H$ and keep six decimals; convert Δm to MeV with 931.5 only at the end.
- Show that A cancels when proving constant nuclear density.
- Balance A and Z in every nuclear equation; Q = (mass lost) × 931.5 MeV.
- Explain "why both release energy" with the maximum of the B/A curve and the direction in which each type of nucleus moves.
- Each reactor part gets one function; fusion needs a high temperature because of the Coulomb repulsion.

cards.front_md: What is a nucleon?
cards.back_md: A proton or a neutron inside a nucleus.

cards.front_md: Meaning of Z, N and A?
cards.back_md: Z protons, N neutrons, A = Z + N nucleons.

cards.front_md: Isotopes, isobars, isotones?
cards.back_md: Same Z; same A; same N.

cards.front_md: ¹³C and ¹³N: isotopes, isobars or isotones?
cards.back_md: Isobars: both have A = 13 (Z = 6 and 7, so N = 7 and 6).

cards.front_md: Define the unified atomic mass unit.
cards.back_md: One twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom: 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

cards.front_md: Formula for the radius of a nucleus?
Why does R ∝ A^(1/3) mean a constant density?
cards.back_md: Volume ∝ R³ ∝ A, so volume is proportional to mass: mass/volume is the same for all nuclei.

cards.front_md: Order of magnitude of nuclear density?
cards.back_md: About 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, the same for every nucleus.

cards.front_md: Size of a nucleus compared with its atom?
cards.back_md: Radius about 10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻¹⁴ m against 10⁻¹⁰ m: about 10⁴ to 10⁵ times smaller.

cards.front_md: What holds a nucleus together?
cards.back_md: The strong nuclear force: short-range, attractive, equal between any pair of nucleons.

cards.front_md: Mass–energy relation?
cards.back_md: $E = mc^2$: mass m is equivalent to energy mc².

cards.front_md: Energy equivalent of 1 u?
Define mass defect.
cards.back_md: Total mass of the separate nucleons minus the mass of the nucleus.

cards.front_md: Mass defect from atomic masses?
cards.back_md: $\Delta m = Zm_H + (A - Z)m_n - M_{\text{atom}}$ (electron masses cancel).

cards.front_md: Define binding energy.
cards.back_md: Energy equivalent of the mass defect: needed to separate a nucleus into its nucleons, or released when it forms.

cards.front_md: Binding energy in MeV from Δm in u?
cards.back_md: B = Δm × 931.5 MeV.

cards.front_md: Pair production: threshold and condition?
cards.back_md: Photon energy ≥ 2mₑc² = 1.022 MeV, near a nucleus (momentum).

cards.front_md: Why must a nucleus be near for pair production?
cards.back_md: To take up momentum, so energy and momentum are both conserved.

cards.front_md: Annihilation of an electron and a positron at rest?
cards.back_md: Two photons of 0.511 MeV each, in opposite directions.

cards.front_md: Where is the binding energy per nucleon greatest?
cards.back_md: About 8.8 MeV near A = 56–62 (iron, nickel).

cards.front_md: Which nuclei are most stable?
cards.back_md: Middle-order nuclei (A about 50 to 80): highest B/A.

cards.front_md: Why does B/A fall for heavy nuclei?
cards.back_md: The long-range electrostatic repulsion between protons grows faster than the number of nucleons.

cards.front_md: Why do fission and fusion both release energy?
cards.back_md: Both move nuclei towards the peak of the B/A curve, increasing the total binding energy.

cards.front_md: Energy from a heavy nucleus splitting into halves?
cards.back_md: A × (B/A of the halves − B/A of the heavy nucleus), about 200 MeV for A = 236.

cards.front_md: Define nuclear fission.
cards.back_md: A heavy nucleus splits into two middle-order nuclei, with neutrons and about 200 MeV released.

cards.front_md: Controlled versus uncontrolled chain reaction?
cards.back_md: Controlled: one further fission per fission on average (reactor). Uncontrolled: more than one (bomb).

cards.front_md: Functions of moderator, control rods, coolant, shielding?
cards.back_md: Slows neutrons; absorbs neutrons to regulate the rate; carries heat away; absorbs neutrons and gamma rays.

cards.front_md: Define nuclear fusion.
cards.back_md: Two light nuclei join into a heavier one, with energy released.

cards.front_md: Why is a very high temperature needed for fusion?
cards.back_md: To give nuclei enough energy to overcome their mutual electrostatic repulsion (Coulomb barrier).

cards.front_md: Source of the Sun’s energy?
cards.back_md: Fusion of four hydrogen nuclei into one helium nucleus: about 26.7 MeV each (thermonuclear energy).

questions.stem_md: Isotones are nuclides with the same number of neutrons. Which of these pairs of nuclides are isotones?

options.text_md: ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl
³⁷₁₇Cl and ³⁹₁₉K
⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₂₀Ca
¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C

questions.solution_md: N = A − Z. ³⁷₁₇Cl has 37 − 17 = 20 neutrons and ³⁹₁₉K has 39 − 19 = 20: isotones. The chlorine pair and the carbon pair share Z (isotopes); the argon–calcium pair shares A (isobars) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The nucleus of copper-64 (⁶⁴₂₉Cu) has radius R. A nucleus of radius R/2 has a mass number of
questions.solution_md: $R \propto A^{1/3}$, so $\dfrac{A'}{64} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{8}$ and $A' = 8$ — option (d). Halving A (32) or quartering it (16) would only reduce the radius by 2^(1/3) or 4^(1/3).

questions.stem_md: The unified atomic mass unit (u) is defined as

options.text_md: the mass of one proton at rest
one twelfth of the mass of the nucleus of a carbon-12 atom
one sixteenth of the mass of a neutral oxygen-16 atom
one twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom

questions.solution_md: By definition 1 u is 1/12 of the mass of a neutral ¹²C atom (nucleus plus its six electrons), so the atomic mass of ¹²C is exactly 12 u — option (d). A proton is 1.007276 u, and the older oxygen-16 scale is no longer used.

questions.stem_md: Carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) and oxygen-16 (¹⁶₈O) each have 8 neutrons but different numbers of protons. Nuclides related in this way are called ___.
questions.solution_md: **Isotones**: N = 14 − 6 = 16 − 8 = 8, with different Z (6 and 8).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Two isotopes of an element have the same nuclear radius, because they have the same number of protons.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The radius depends on the mass number: $R = R_0A^{1/3}$. Isotopes have the same Z but different A (different numbers of neutrons), so the heavier isotope has the larger radius.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The mass density of the nucleus of uranium-238 (²³⁸₉₂U) is about the same as that of helium-4 (⁴₂He).

**Reason (R):** The radius of a nucleus is directly proportional to its mass number.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true, R is false. The radius grows only as the cube root of the mass number, $R = R_0A^{1/3}$; that makes the volume, not the radius, proportional to $A$, and since the mass is also proportional to $A$, every nucleus has about the same density (about $2.3 \times 10^{17}$ kg m⁻³) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Find the radius of the nucleus of tin-120 (¹²⁰₅₀Sn) in fm, to 3 significant figures. (R₀ = 1.2 fm)
A nucleus has a radius of 5.0 fm. Taking R₀ = 1.25 fm, find its mass number.

A matchbox measures 4.0 cm × 3.0 cm × 1.5 cm. Nuclear matter has the density 3m/(4πR₀³) of a nucleus. Taking R₀ = 1.25 fm and the mass of a nucleon as m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, find the mass of nuclear matter that would fill the box, in units of 10¹² kg (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\rho = \dfrac{3 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{4\pi(1.25 \times 10^{-15})^3} = 2.04 \times 10^{17}$ kg m⁻³. Volume $= 4.0 \times 3.0 \times 1.5 = 18$ cm³ $= 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ m³. Mass $= 2.04 \times 10^{17} \times 1.8 \times 10^{-5} = 3.67 \times 10^{12}$ kg $= 3.67$ in units of $10^{12}$ kg (about 3.7 thousand million tonnes).

questions.stem_md: The radius of a zinc atom is 1.40 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. What fraction of the volume of the atom is taken up by its nucleus ⁶⁴₃₀Zn? Give the answer in units of 10⁻¹⁴ (3 significant figures). (R₀ = 1.2 fm)
questions.solution_md: Nuclear radius $R = 1.2 \times 64^{1/3} = 4.8$ fm $= 4.8 \times 10^{-15}$ m. Fraction of volume $= \left(\dfrac{R}{R_{\text{atom}}}\right)^3 = \left(\dfrac{4.8 \times 10^{-15}}{1.40 \times 10^{-10}}\right)^3 = (3.43 \times 10^{-5})^3 = 4.03 \times 10^{-14}$; in units of $10^{-14}$ this is $\dfrac{4.03 \times 10^{-14}}{10^{-14}} = 4.03$: the atom is almost entirely empty space.

questions.stem_md: Match each nuclide in Column A with the number of neutrons in its nucleus in Column B.

options.text_md: ¹⁴₆C
²³₁₁Na
⁵⁹₂₇Co
²⁰⁷₈₂Pb

questions.stem_md: Name the relation between the nuclides in each pair, with a reason: (a) ²⁴₁₁Na and ²⁴₁₂Mg; (b) ³²₁₅P and ³³₁₆S.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Isobars: both have mass number 24 (same number of nucleons) but different atomic numbers, 11 and 12. (b) Isotones: phosphorus-32 has 32 − 15 = 17 neutrons and sulphur-33 has 33 − 16 = 17 neutrons, the same number, while their proton numbers differ.

questions.solution_md: Same A → isobars; same N → isotones.

questions.stem_md: Using the empirical formula for the radius of a nucleus, prove that nuclear matter has the same density whatever the mass number of the nucleus, and evaluate that density. (R₀ = 1.2 fm, mass of a nucleon 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)

answer.model_answer_md: A nucleus of mass number A has mass $\approx Am$ and radius $R = R_0A^{1/3}$, so its volume is $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3A$. Then $\rho = \dfrac{Am}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3A} = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}$: A cancels, so ρ is the same for every nucleus. Numerically $\rho = \dfrac{3 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{4\pi(1.2 \times 10^{-15})^3} = 2.31 \times 10^{17}$ kg m⁻³.

questions.solution_md: Mass ∝ A and volume ∝ A, so ρ = 3m/(4πR₀³).

marking_scheme.step: A cancels: ρ = 3m/(4πR₀³), independent of A

questions.stem_md: Define the unified atomic mass unit. Using 1 u = 1.66054 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 2.99792 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and 1 eV = 1.60218 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, show that the energy equivalent of 1 u is about 931.5 MeV.

answer.model_answer_md: One unified atomic mass unit is one twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom. $E = mc^2 = 1.66054 \times 10^{-27} \times (2.99792 \times 10^{8})^2 = 1.492 \times 10^{-10}$ J $= \dfrac{1.492 \times 10^{-10}}{1.60218 \times 10^{-13}}$ MeV $= 931.5$ MeV $\approx 931.5$ MeV.

questions.solution_md: Definition; E = mc²; convert joules to MeV.

marking_scheme.step: 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a neutral ¹²C atom

questions.stem_md: For a nucleus of mass number $A$ and atomic number $Z$ and mass $M$, with proton mass $m_p$ and neutron mass $m_n$, the mass defect is

options.text_md: $M - Zm_p - (A - Z)m_n$
$Zm_p + (A - Z)m_n - M$
$(A - Z)m_p + Zm_n - M$
$A(m_p + m_n) - M$

questions.solution_md: The mass defect is the mass of the separate nucleons ($Z$ protons and $A - Z$ neutrons) minus the mass of the nucleus — option (b). The reverse order would be negative; the other two use the wrong number of each nucleon.

questions.stem_md: The binding energy of a nucleus is

options.text_md: the energy needed to remove the electrons from the atom
the kinetic energy with which the nucleons move about inside the nucleus
the energy needed to separate the nucleus completely into its free protons and neutrons
the total energy released when the nucleus emits one gamma ray

questions.solution_md: Binding energy = (mass defect) × c²: the work needed to pull all the nucleons apart, equal to the energy released when they come together to form the nucleus — option (c). Removing electrons is ionisation, which involves eV, not MeV.

questions.stem_md: Pair production needs a photon of at least 1.022 MeV. Taking hc = 1240 MeV fm, the longest wavelength of a photon that can produce an electron–positron pair is about
questions.solution_md: $\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{hc}{E_{\min}} = \dfrac{1240\ \text{MeV fm}}{1.022\ \text{MeV}} = 1213$ fm $= 1.21$ pm — option (a). 2.43 pm is the wavelength of one annihilation photon (0.511 MeV); 0.61 pm would need 2.04 MeV.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A photon of energy 0.80 MeV cannot produce an electron–positron pair, however close it passes to a nucleus.

**Reason (R):** The rest energy of an electron and a positron together is 1.022 MeV, more than the photon’s energy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: the photon cannot supply the 2 × 0.511 = 1.022 MeV needed just to create the two particles at rest, and the nucleus can only take up momentum, not provide energy — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A tightly compressed spring has very slightly more mass than the same spring when it is relaxed.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The extra elastic energy stored in the spring has an equivalent mass E/c² (about 10⁻¹⁷ kg or less for ordinary springs: far too small to weigh), by E = mc².

questions.stem_md: The atomic mass of calcium-40 (⁴⁰₂₀Ca) is 39.962591 u. Find its binding energy in MeV, to 3 significant figures. (m_H = 1.007825 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV)
The atomic mass of magnesium-24 (²⁴₁₂Mg) is 23.985042 u. Find its mass defect in u, to 4 significant figures. (m_H = 1.007825 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u)

Calcium-40 (⁴⁰₂₀Ca, atomic mass 39.962591 u) is split into calcium-39 (³⁹₂₀Ca, 38.970710 u) and a neutron. What energy must be supplied to remove the neutron, in MeV (3 significant figures)? (mₙ = 1.008665 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV)
questions.solution_md: Mass after $= 38.970710 + 1.008665 = 39.979375$ u; the extra mass is $\Delta m = 39.979375 - 39.962591 = 0.0167840$ u. Energy needed $= 0.0167840 \times 931.5 = 15.63$ MeV. (The nucleus must be given this much energy: it is the binding energy of the last neutron.)

questions.stem_md: The atomic masses of tritium (³₁H) and helium-3 (³₂He) are 3.016049 u and 3.016029 u. Find how much larger the binding energy of tritium is than that of helium-3, in MeV (3 significant figures). (m_H = 1.007825 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV)
questions.solution_md: Tritium: $\Delta m = 1.007825 + 2 \times 1.008665 - 3.016049 = 0.00910600$ u. Helium-3: $\Delta m = 2 \times 1.007825 + 1.008665 - 3.016029 = 0.00828600$ u. Difference $= 0.000820000$ u $\times 931.5 = 0.764$ MeV. Helium-3, with two protons repelling each other, is slightly less tightly bound.

questions.stem_md: Find the mass equivalent of the energy of 1.0 MeV, in units of 10⁻³⁰ kg (3 significant figures). (1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.solution_md: $m = \dfrac{E}{c^2} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-13}}{(3.0 \times 10^{8})^2} = 1.78 \times 10^{-30}$ kg $= 1.78$ in units of $10^{-30}$ kg (about twice the mass of an electron, 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg).

questions.stem_md: A 100 W lamp burns for one year (3.15 × 10⁷ s). What mass would have to be converted completely into energy to supply this, in micrograms (3 significant figures)? (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.solution_md: $E = Pt = 100 \times 3.15 \times 10^{7} = 3.15 \times 10^{9}$ J. $m = \dfrac{E}{c^2} = \dfrac{3.15 \times 10^{9}}{(3.0 \times 10^{8})^2} = 3.50 \times 10^{-8}$ kg $= 35.0$ μg (1 μg = 10⁻⁹ kg): a speck of dust.

questions.stem_md: A photon of energy 4.20 MeV produces an electron–positron pair in the field of a nucleus. Find the total kinetic energy of the pair, in MeV (3 significant figures). (mₑc² = 0.511 MeV; ignore the recoil of the nucleus)
questions.solution_md: Energy to create the pair at rest: $2 \times 0.511 = 1.022$ MeV. Kinetic energy of the pair $= 4.20 - 1.022 = 3.178$ MeV $\approx 3.18$ MeV.

questions.stem_md: An electron and a positron at rest annihilate and produce two photons. Find the wavelength of each photon, in pm (1 pm = 10³ fm), to 3 significant figures. (hc = 1240 MeV fm, mₑc² = 0.511 MeV)
questions.solution_md: Each photon takes the rest energy of one particle, 0.511 MeV. $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E} = \dfrac{1240}{0.511} = 2427$ fm $= 2.43$ pm.

questions.stem_md: Explain, using E = mc², why the mass of a helium-4 nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its two protons and two neutrons, and what the missing mass represents.

answer.model_answer_md: When nucleons bind, energy is released, and by E = mc² the system loses mass equal to that energy divided by c². So the nucleus weighs less than its separate parts. The missing mass, the mass defect, equals the binding energy divided by c²: the energy needed to pull the nucleus apart again.

questions.solution_md: Energy released on formation carries away mass Δm = B/c².

marking_scheme.step: Energy released when nucleons bind, so the mass falls by E/c²
Mass defect ↔ binding energy: needed to separate the nucleons

questions.stem_md: Why does the annihilation of an electron and a positron at rest give two photons, not one? State the energy of each photon.

answer.model_answer_md: Before annihilation the total momentum is zero. A single photon always carries momentum, so one photon could not conserve it. Two photons moving in opposite directions have momenta that cancel, so momentum is conserved. The rest energy 2 × 0.511 MeV is shared equally: each photon has 0.511 MeV.

questions.solution_md: Momentum conservation requires two photons in opposite directions, 0.511 MeV each.

marking_scheme.step: Initial momentum zero; one photon would have momentum; two opposite photons cancel

questions.stem_md: What is pair production? State the minimum photon energy needed, and explain why the process happens only in the electric field of a nucleus.

answer.model_answer_md: In pair production a gamma-ray photon changes into an electron and a positron, so energy becomes mass. The photon must supply at least the rest energy of the two particles, 2mₑc² = 2 × 0.511 = 1.022 MeV; any extra becomes their kinetic energy. A photon alone cannot do it, since energy and momentum could not both be conserved. A nearby nucleus takes up the extra momentum, with almost no energy.

questions.solution_md: γ → e⁻ + e⁺ near a nucleus; threshold 1.022 MeV; nucleus for momentum.

marking_scheme.step: Nucleus needed to take up momentum

questions.stem_md: The atomic mass of helium-4 is 4.002603 u. Calculate (a) its mass defect and (b) its binding energy, and (c) say what the binding energy means. (m_H = 1.007825 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV)

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\Delta m = 2 \times 1.007825 + 2 \times 1.008665 - 4.002603 = 4.032980 - 4.002603 = 0.0303770$ u. (b) $B = 0.0303770 \times 931.5 = 28.30$ MeV. (c) It is the energy that must be supplied to separate the nucleus into two protons and two neutrons (and the energy released when they join).

questions.solution_md: Δm = 2m_H + 2mₙ − M; B = Δm × 931.5.

marking_scheme.step: Energy needed to separate (released on formation)

questions.stem_md: (a) Define mass defect and binding energy of a nucleus, and state how they are related. [2] (b) The atomic mass of silicon-28 (²⁸₁₄Si) is 27.976927 u. Find its mass defect and its binding energy. [2] (c) Find the binding energy per nucleon, and state whether silicon-28 is more tightly bound per nucleon than neon-20, for which it is 8.03 MeV. [1] (m_H = 1.007825 u, mₙ = 1.008665 u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Mass defect: the total mass of the separate nucleons minus the mass of the nucleus. Binding energy: the energy needed to separate the nucleus into its nucleons; $B = \Delta m\,c^2$.

(b) $\Delta m = 14 \times 1.007825 + 14 \times 1.008665 - 27.976927 = 28.230860 - 27.976927 = 0.253933$ u. $B = 0.253933 \times 931.5 = 236.5$ MeV.

(c) $\dfrac{B}{A} = \dfrac{236.5}{28} = 8.45$ MeV per nucleon, which is greater than 8.03 MeV, so silicon-28 is more tightly bound per nucleon.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; Δm and B; B/A.

marking_scheme.step: Definition of mass defect and of binding energy
B/A = 8.45 MeV > 8.03 MeV: more tightly bound

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe pair production, saying what is needed for it to happen and what the minimum photon energy is. [2] (b) A photon of energy 2.30 MeV produces a pair near a nucleus. Find the total kinetic energy of the electron and the positron. [1] (c) The positron later meets an electron and both annihilate at rest. State the number and the energy of the photons produced, and find their wavelength. [2] (mₑc² = 0.511 MeV, hc = 1240 MeV fm)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A gamma-ray photon passing close to a nucleus changes into an electron and a positron; the nucleus takes up momentum, so that energy and momentum are both conserved. The photon must have at least 2mₑc² = 1.022 MeV.

(b) Kinetic energy of the pair $= 2.30 - 1.022 = 1.278$ MeV.

(c) Two photons, in opposite directions, each of energy 0.511 MeV. $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E} = \dfrac{1240}{0.511} = 2427$ fm $= 2.43$ pm.

questions.solution_md: Threshold 1.022 MeV; K = E − 1.022; two 0.511 MeV photons.

marking_scheme.step: Photon → e⁻ + e⁺ near a nucleus (momentum)
Two photons of 0.511 MeV in opposite directions

questions.stem_md: On the graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number, nucleus P lies far to the left of the maximum and nucleus Q far to the right of it. Energy can be released if

options.text_md: P splits into two smaller nuclei, or Q fuses with a heavier nucleus
only P can release energy, by fusion; Q cannot release energy by any nuclear process
P fuses with another light nucleus, or Q splits into two middle-order nuclei
only Q can release energy, by fission; P cannot release energy by any nuclear process

questions.solution_md: Energy is released when nuclei move towards the maximum of the curve (higher B/A). P, on the rising part, gains B/A by fusing into a heavier nucleus; Q, on the falling part, gains B/A by splitting into middle-order fragments. Both are possible — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a massive star, the release of energy by fusion stops when the core has become mostly iron-group nuclei. This is because

options.text_md: iron nuclei are radioactive and break up as fast as they form
iron nuclei have too few protons to repel one another and fuse
iron-group nuclei have the maximum binding energy per nucleon, so fusing them would take in energy instead of releasing it
the temperature of the core always falls below 10⁷ K once iron forms

questions.solution_md: Fusion releases energy only while the product has a higher binding energy per nucleon than the reactants. The curve peaks at iron and nickel (A about 56–62), so fusing them moves nuclei down the curve: energy would have to be supplied — option (c).

questions.stem_md: For mass numbers above about 60, the binding energy per nucleon falls as A increases, mainly because

options.text_md: the strong nuclear force becomes repulsive between nucleons in large nuclei
neutrons in large nuclei are heavier than neutrons in small nuclei
the strong force has a longer range in heavier nuclei and the nucleons crowd together
the electrostatic repulsion between protons, which acts across the whole nucleus, grows faster than the number of nucleons

questions.solution_md: The strong force is short-range and acts only between near neighbours, so it adds the same binding per nucleon; the electrostatic repulsion acts between every pair of protons, so its total grows faster than A and lowers B/A — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Per nucleon, the fusion of light nuclei releases more energy than the fission of heavy nuclei.

**Reason (R):** On the graph of binding energy per nucleon, the curve rises much more steeply at small mass numbers than it falls at large mass numbers.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: fusing hydrogen isotopes into helium raises B/A by several MeV per nucleon (1.1 → 7.07 MeV), but fission of uranium raises it by only about 0.9 MeV (7.6 → 8.5) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Two nuclei of nickel-62, the nuclide with the greatest binding energy per nucleon, fusing to form a single nucleus of mass number 124 would release energy.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. A nucleus with A = 124 lies to the right of the maximum, so its binding energy per nucleon is lower than that of nickel-62; the total binding energy would fall, so energy would have to be supplied.

questions.stem_md: A heavy nucleus of mass number 224 has a binding energy per nucleon of 7.62 MeV. It splits into two equal fragments, each with a binding energy per nucleon of 8.46 MeV. Estimate the energy released, in MeV (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Each fragment has A = 112. Binding energy before: $224 \times 7.62 = 1706.88$ MeV; after: $2 \times 112 \times 8.46 = 1895.04$ MeV. Energy released $= 1895.04 - 1706.88 = 188$ MeV.

questions.stem_md: In the very hot core of a massive star, two silicon-28 nuclei (binding energy per nucleon 8.45 MeV) can fuse to form one nucleus of nickel-56 (binding energy per nucleon 8.64 MeV). Estimate the energy released in one such fusion, in MeV (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Before: $2 \times 28 \times 8.45 = 473.20$ MeV. After: $56 \times 8.64 = 483.84$ MeV. Energy released $= 483.84 - 473.20 = 10.6$ MeV (equivalently $56 \times 0.19$).

questions.stem_md: A nucleus of mass number 235 (binding energy per nucleon 7.59 MeV) splits into two unequal fragments, of mass numbers 95 (8.70 MeV per nucleon) and 140 (8.40 MeV per nucleon). Find the energy released, in MeV (3 significant figures).
Explain why a star cannot obtain energy by fusing iron nuclei, although it can obtain it by fusing hydrogen or helium nuclei.

answer.model_answer_md: Fusion releases energy only if the binding energy per nucleon increases. For hydrogen and helium the curve rises steeply, so the products are more tightly bound per nucleon. Iron is at the maximum of the curve, so fusing iron nuclei gives a heavier nucleus with lower binding energy per nucleon, and energy would have to be supplied instead.

questions.solution_md: B/A rises for light nuclei, peaks at iron.

marking_scheme.step: Fusion releases energy only when B/A increases; true for light nuclei
Iron is at the maximum: fusing it lowers B/A, absorbing energy

questions.stem_md: A student argues: “Fission of uranium releases energy because the nucleus splits. Fusion joins nuclei together, the opposite process, so it must absorb energy.” Evaluate this argument using the binding energy per nucleon curve.

answer.model_answer_md: The argument is wrong. What matters is not splitting or joining but the binding energy per nucleon. Uranium lies to the right of the maximum, so splitting moves its fragments up the curve towards iron and releases energy. Hydrogen and other light nuclei lie to the left of the maximum, so joining them also moves the product up the curve, to a higher binding energy per nucleon, and releases energy as well.

questions.solution_md: Energy is released when nuclei move towards the maximum of the B/A curve, from either side.

marking_scheme.step: What matters is the change in binding energy per nucleon, not splitting or joining
Heavy nuclei on the right: fission moves them up the curve
Light nuclei on the left: fusion also moves them up, so energy is released

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw (describe in words) the graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number, marking the maximum and the regions of light and heavy nuclei, and state which nuclei are the most stable. [2] (b) Use the graph to explain why energy is released both when a very heavy nucleus splits and when two very light nuclei join. [1] (c) A nucleus of mass number 232 with a binding energy per nucleon of 7.60 MeV splits into two equal fragments, each with 8.40 MeV per nucleon. Estimate the energy released. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) B/A (vertical axis, in MeV) rises steeply from about 1 MeV for hydrogen-2 through a bump at helium-4 (7.07 MeV) to a maximum of about 8.8 MeV at A about 56–62 (iron, nickel), then falls slowly to about 7.6 MeV for uranium. The middle-order nuclei near the maximum are the most stable.

(b) Both processes move nuclei towards the maximum: a heavy nucleus splits into middle-order fragments with higher B/A, and light nuclei fuse into a heavier nucleus with higher B/A. The total binding energy increases, and the difference is released.

(c) Before: $232 \times 7.60 = 1763.20$ MeV. After: $232 \times 8.40 = 1948.80$ MeV. Energy released $= 185.6$ MeV $\approx 186$ MeV.

questions.solution_md: Peak near A = 56–62; both move towards the peak; E = A(b₂ − b₁).

marking_scheme.step: Graph: steep rise, maximum about 8.8 MeV near A = 56–62, slow fall
Most stable: the middle-order nuclei at the maximum
Both fission and fusion move nuclei towards the maximum, raising total binding energy

questions.stem_md: In the fission reaction ¹₀n + ²³⁵₉₂U → ¹⁴⁴₅₆Ba + ⁸⁹₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n, the value of x is
questions.solution_md: Nucleon number: 1 + 235 = 144 + 89 + x, so x = 236 − 233 = 3. Charge: 92 = 56 + 36 balances with no charge carried by the neutrons — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A moderator slows neutrons down by collisions. Which of these materials would be the poorest moderator?

options.text_md: graphite, whose carbon nuclei are about 12 times as heavy as a neutron
heavy water, whose deuterium nuclei are about twice as heavy as a neutron
lead, whose nuclei are very much heavier than a neutron
ordinary water, whose hydrogen nuclei have almost the same mass as a neutron

questions.solution_md: A neutron loses a large share of its energy only in collisions with nuclei of comparable mass (like a ball hitting a ball of equal mass). Off a very heavy lead nucleus it bounces back with almost all its energy, so lead is the poorest moderator — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a reactor that burns natural-type uranium fuel, the moderator is accidentally drained away while the fuel stays in place. The chain reaction will

options.text_md: speed up, because there is nothing left to absorb the fission neutrons
speed up, because fast neutrons are more likely than slow ones to cause fission in uranium-235
be unaffected, because the control rods alone decide how many neutrons are produced
die away, because the fast neutrons are no longer slowed enough to cause fission in uranium-235

questions.solution_md: Slow (thermal) neutrons are far more likely than fast ones to cause fission in U-235. Without the moderator the neutrons stay fast, fewer fissions follow, and the chain reaction fades — option (d). The control rods only absorb neutrons; they do not slow them.

questions.stem_md: The thick concrete and steel walls built around a nuclear reactor core mainly serve to

options.text_md: slow the neutrons so that they cause more fissions inside the core
absorb the neutrons and gamma rays that would otherwise reach people outside
carry the heat from the core to the turbine
remove the excess neutrons so that the chain reaction stays controlled

questions.solution_md: This is the shielding. Slowing neutrons is the moderator, carrying heat away is the coolant, and removing neutrons to control the rate is the job of the control rods — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a nuclear reactor operating at a steady power, every neutron released in a fission goes on to cause another fission.

**Reason (R):** For a steady chain reaction, on average only one neutron from each fission must go on to cause another fission.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false, R is true. Each fission releases two or three neutrons; if all of them caused further fissions the rate would multiply from one generation to the next. At steady power only one per fission does so on average, and the surplus is absorbed by the control rods and other materials or escapes — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The power of a reactor is regulated by pushing rods of cadmium or boron, which absorb neutrons strongly, further into the core. These are called ___ rods.
questions.solution_md: **Control rods**: pushed in, they absorb more neutrons and lower the rate of fission; pulled out, they let it rise.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Fast neutrons are more likely than slow neutrons to cause the fission of a uranium-235 nucleus.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Slow (thermal) neutrons are much more likely to be captured by a U-235 nucleus and cause fission; that is why a moderator is used to slow the fast neutrons released in fission.

questions.stem_md: Find the energy released, in MeV (3 significant figures), when a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits as ¹₀n + ²³⁵₉₂U → ¹⁴⁰₅₅Cs + ⁹³₃₇Rb + 3 ¹₀n. (Atomic masses: ²³⁵U 235.043930 u, ¹⁴⁰Cs 139.917283 u, ⁹³Rb 92.922039 u; mₙ = 1.008665 u; 1 u = 931.5 MeV)

marking_scheme.step: Masses before 236.052595 u and after 235.865317 u

questions.stem_md: A uranium nucleus at rest splits into a barium fragment (mass number 141) and a krypton fragment (mass number 92) that fly apart with a total kinetic energy of 165 MeV. Taking the mass of each fragment as proportional to its mass number, find the kinetic energy of the krypton fragment, in MeV (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Momentum is conserved and the nucleus started at rest, so the fragments have equal and opposite momenta p. Then $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m} \propto \dfrac{1}{m}$: $\dfrac{K_{Kr}}{K_{Ba}} = \dfrac{141}{92}$. With $K_{Kr} + K_{Ba} = 165$ MeV: $K_{Kr} = 165 \times \dfrac{141}{141 + 92} = 99.8$ MeV (and $K_{Ba} = 65.2$ MeV).

marking_scheme.step: Equal momenta, so K ∝ 1/m: K_Kr : K_Ba = 141 : 92

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an uncontrolled and a controlled chain reaction in terms of what happens to the neutrons released in each fission. Give one use of each.

answer.model_answer_md: In an uncontrolled chain reaction more than one neutron per fission causes another fission, so the fissions multiply and the energy is released almost at once: a nuclear bomb. In a controlled one, on average only one neutron per fission causes another; the rest escape or are absorbed by control rods, so the power stays steady: a reactor.

questions.solution_md: More than one neutron continues (bomb); exactly one continues (reactor).

questions.stem_md: In a nuclear reactor, name the part that (i) slows the fast neutrons, (ii) absorbs neutrons to regulate the rate of the chain reaction, and (iii) takes the heat out of the core. Give one material used for each.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The moderator slows the fast neutrons by collisions, so that they can cause fission of uranium-235; heavy water or graphite is used. (ii) The control rods absorb neutrons; pushing them in lowers the rate of fission and pulling them out raises it; they are made of cadmium or boron. (iii) The coolant carries the heat from the core to the steam generator; water, liquid sodium or carbon dioxide may be used.

questions.stem_md: Why must the fast neutrons released in fission be slowed down in a reactor that uses uranium-235? What property should a good moderator have, and why is water or graphite suitable?

answer.model_answer_md: Slow neutrons are much more likely than fast ones to be captured by uranium-235 and cause fission, so the fast neutrons from one fission must be slowed before they can cause the next. A good moderator has light nuclei, because a neutron loses most energy colliding with a nucleus of similar mass, and absorbs few neutrons. Water, heavy water and graphite have light nuclei and absorb few neutrons.

questions.solution_md: Slow neutrons cause fission; light nuclei slow neutrons.

questions.stem_md: (a) What is nuclear fission? [1] (b) Find the energy released in the fission ¹₀n + ²³⁵₉₂U → ¹⁴⁰₅₅Cs + ⁹³₃₇Rb + x ¹₀n, after finding x. (Atomic masses: ²³⁵U 235.043930 u, ¹⁴⁰Cs 139.917283 u, ⁹³Rb 92.922039 u; mₙ = 1.008665 u; 1 u = 931.5 MeV) [2] (c) Explain how the chain reaction is kept controlled in a reactor. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The splitting of a heavy nucleus, after it absorbs a slow neutron, into two middle-order nuclei, with the release of neutrons and a large amount of energy.

(b) Nucleon number: $1 + 235 = 140 + 93 + x$, so $x = 3$. Mass before $= 236.052595$ u; after $= 235.865317$ u; $\Delta m = 0.187278$ u; $Q = 0.187278 \times 931.5 = 174.4$ MeV.

(c) Each fission releases two or three neutrons, but only one on average must cause a further fission. Control rods of cadmium or boron absorb the surplus neutrons; pushing them in lowers the rate and pulling them out raises it. The moderator slows the neutrons so that they can cause fission, and the rods are moved to keep exactly one neutron per fission carrying on.

questions.solution_md: x = 3; Q = Δm × 931.5; control rods absorb the surplus neutrons.

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe, with a labelled diagram (described in words), the main parts of a nuclear reactor and give the function of the fuel, moderator, control rods, coolant and shielding. [3] (b) What would happen to the rate of fission if the control rods were pushed fully into the core, and why? [1] (c) Why can a reactor not explode like a nuclear bomb? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Fuel rods of uranium enriched in U-235 stand in the core, surrounded by the moderator (heavy water or graphite) that slows the fast neutrons so they can cause fission. Control rods of cadmium or boron slide in and out between the fuel rods to absorb neutrons and regulate the rate. A coolant (water or liquid sodium) is pumped through the core and carries the heat to a heat exchanger, where steam is made for a turbine. Thick concrete and steel shielding surrounds the reactor and absorbs neutrons and gamma rays.

(b) The fission rate would fall and the reactor would shut down, because the rods absorb so many neutrons that fewer than one neutron per fission causes another fission.

(c) The fuel is only slightly enriched in U-235 and the control rods keep the number of neutrons steady, so the chain reaction cannot multiply as it does in a bomb, which uses highly enriched fuel in a compact mass with nothing to absorb the neutrons.

options.text_md: one helium nucleus splits into four hydrogen nuclei, absorbing energy
four hydrogen nuclei are converted into one helium nucleus, with two positrons, two neutrinos and energy released

questions.stem_md: In a hydrogen bomb, the very high temperature needed for the fusion of hydrogen isotopes is obtained from

options.text_md: the explosion of a fission bomb
burning chemical explosives such as TNT
compressing the hydrogen with a piston
the radioactive decay of the hydrogen isotopes themselves

questions.solution_md: Only a fission explosion produces temperatures of millions of kelvin, so the hydrogen bomb has a fission bomb as its trigger — option (a). Chemical explosives and pistons cannot reach such temperatures.

questions.stem_md: At the temperature of the Sun’s core (about 1.5 × 10⁷ K) the mean thermal energy of a proton is only about 2 keV, far below the roughly 0.6 MeV needed to bring two protons together. Fusion still goes on in the core mainly because

options.text_md: a tiny fraction of the protons have energies far above the mean, and there are enormous numbers of protons in the core
the protons in the core have no electric charge
gravity switches off the repulsion between the protons
the thermal energy of every proton in the core is actually above 0.6 MeV

questions.solution_md: The protons have a spread of energies; the tiny fraction in the high-energy tail, in a core with an enormous number of protons, is enough to keep fusion going at a steady rate — option (a). The protons are charged and repel; the mean energy really is only about 2 keV.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Nuclear fusion needs temperatures of millions of kelvin.

**Reason (R):** When two light nuclei fuse, the binding energy per nucleon of the product is greater than that of the nuclei that fused.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A. R explains why fusion releases energy. The high temperature is needed because the positive nuclei must approach within about 10⁻¹⁵ m against their electrostatic repulsion, and only very fast nuclei can climb that Coulomb barrier — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two deuterium nuclei (each of mass number 2, charge +e) are brought together until they just touch. Taking each nuclear radius as R₀A^(1/3) with R₀ = 1.2 fm, find the electrostatic potential energy of the pair at that moment, in MeV (3 significant figures). (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J)
questions.solution_md: Radius of each nucleus $= 1.2 \times 2^{1/3} = 1.512$ fm, so the centres are $2R = 3.024$ fm $= 3.024 \times 10^{-15}$ m apart. $U = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{3.024 \times 10^{-15}} = 7.62 \times 10^{-14}$ J $= \dfrac{7.62 \times 10^{-14}}{1.6 \times 10^{-13}} = 0.476$ MeV.

questions.stem_md: Find the temperature at which the mean kinetic energy of a gas particle, (3/2)kT, equals 0.476 MeV, the potential energy of two touching deuterium nuclei. Give the answer in units of 10⁹ K (3 significant figures). (k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J)
questions.solution_md: $0.476$ MeV $= 0.476 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13} = 7.62 \times 10^{-14}$ J. $\dfrac{3}{2}kT = 7.62 \times 10^{-14}$ gives $T = \dfrac{2 \times 7.62 \times 10^{-14}}{3 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23}} = 3.68 \times 10^{9}$ K, so $T/10^{9} = 3.68$ in units of $10^{9}$ K. Real fusion starts at a far lower temperature (about 10⁷–10⁸ K) because the fastest nuclei in the gas carry much more than the mean.

questions.stem_md: The hydrogen nuclei in a cylinder of gas at room temperature collide millions of times a second, yet no fusion takes place. Explain why.

answer.model_answer_md: Hydrogen nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. To fuse they must come within about 10⁻¹⁵ m, which needs kinetic energy of the order of 0.1 MeV or more. At room temperature the mean thermal energy is only about 0.04 eV, so the nuclei turn back far before they get close enough for the strong force to act.

questions.solution_md: Coulomb repulsion; thermal energy far too small.

questions.stem_md: Describe the source of the energy radiated by the Sun. Write the net nuclear reaction, say where the energy comes from, and say why the Sun can keep shining for billions of years.

answer.model_answer_md: The energy comes from fusion in the Sun’s core. Four hydrogen nuclei fuse, in the proton–proton chain, into one helium nucleus with two positrons and two neutrinos: 4 ¹H → ⁴He + 2 e⁺ + 2 ν. The helium nucleus has less mass than four protons; the lost mass, equal to about 26.7 MeV in energy, is released. The Sun’s mass is mostly hydrogen, and each fusion yields a lot of energy, so the supply lasts billions of years.

questions.stem_md: Two protons just touch when their centres are 2.4 fm apart. Calculate the electrostatic potential energy of the pair in MeV, and use it to explain why fusion needs a very high temperature. (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J)

answer.model_answer_md: $U = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{2.4 \times 10^{-15}} = 9.6 \times 10^{-14}$ J $= 0.60$ MeV. Two nuclei must reach this separation, where the strong force takes over, so each pair must have about this much energy to overcome the repulsion. Such energies per particle correspond to enormous temperatures, so the gas must be made extremely hot for any appreciable number of nuclei to fuse.

questions.stem_md: (a) What is nuclear fusion? Explain why it takes place only at very high temperatures. [2] (b) Calculate the energy released in the fusion ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₂He + ¹₀n. (Atomic masses: ²H 2.014102 u, ³He 3.016029 u; mₙ = 1.008665 u; 1 u = 931.5 MeV) [2] (c) Why does a hydrogen bomb need a fission bomb to set it off? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Fusion is the joining of two light nuclei into a heavier nucleus, with the release of energy because the product has a higher binding energy per nucleon. The nuclei repel each other electrically, and must come within about $10^{-15}$ m, where the strong nuclear force acts; only nuclei moving at the very high speeds of a gas at millions of kelvin can overcome the repulsion.

(b) Before: $2 \times 2.014102 = 4.0282040$ u. After: $3.016029 + 1.008665 = 4.0246940$ u. $\Delta m = 0.00351000$ u, so $Q = 0.00351000 \times 931.5 = 3.270$ MeV.

(c) The fusion of hydrogen isotopes needs a temperature of millions of kelvin, which only a fission explosion can supply.

questions.solution_md: Fusion needs high T to beat repulsion; Q = Δm × 931.5; fission gives the temperature.

High T to overcome the electrostatic repulsion
Fission explosion supplies millions of kelvin
